topStories.headline: Shipwreck Cove Playground Opens at Sunset Dunes, Funded Entirely by 1,000 Private Donors
topStories.dek: The 6,000-square-foot pirate-themed play structure debuted at Ocean Beach on September 26, becoming the only playground on the two-mile park.
topStories.body:
Hundreds of families turned out to Sunset Dunes at Kirkham Street on the afternoon of Saturday, September 26 for the ribbon-cutting of Shipwreck Cove, a new pirate-themed playground built into the oceanfront park. <cite index="62-5">Several hundred kids, parents, and people of all walks came to Sunset Dunes at Kirkham Street Saturday afternoon to celebrate the opening of the park's newest feature: the pirate-themed Shipwreck Cove playground.</cite>

<cite index="62-7,62-8,62-9">Shipwreck Cove is a 6,000-square-foot "dune education and playground for kids of all ages and abilities." It was designed and built by Something Labs, an independent collective of engineers and builders, many of whom create exhibits at the Exploratorium. The playground cost $800,000, funded entirely by philanthropists.</cite> <cite index="64-13">Shipwreck Cove was paid for through a fundraiser that came up with $800,000 from 1,000 individuals.</cite>

<cite index="64-10,64-11">The tall tale behind Shipwreck Cove is that a 19th-century wooden sailing ship has washed ashore on Ocean Beach. Young adventurers go up a plank to inspect the mast, climb a rope ladder to the crow's nest, and dig in the sand for sunken treasure — or maybe the skeleton of Billy Bones the pirate.</cite>

<cite index="62-10,62-11">Sunset Dunes drew more than 1.7 million visitors in its first year, and many of them were families. In an initial planning process led by Rec and Park and Friends of Sunset Dunes, a majority of survey respondents said they visit the park with children, and open house attendees asked for more places for kids to play.</cite> <cite index="62-13">Shipwreck Cove operates under a one-year pilot permit, and feedback from families will help inform the park's ongoing community planning process.</cite>

topStories.headline: Prop G Is on the November 3 Ballot — and Reopening the Great Highway Would Cost the City $10 Million
topStories.dek: With the citywide vote now 32 days away, the Controller's Office has put a price tag on reversing the Sunset Dunes park conversion: nearly $10 million upfront and up to $1.9 million every year after.
topStories.body:
<cite index="24-4,24-5">San Francisco voters will have to decide on the fate of the city's westernmost coastal boulevard — again. A proposal to reopen the Great Highway during weekdays has qualified for the ballot this November, threatening Sunset Dunes Park, which opened on the shuttered highway last year.</cite> <cite index="24-6">This will be the third time in four years that San Franciscans have voted on whether or not to allow cars on the highway.</cite>

<cite index="106-10">Prop G would reopen a two-mile stretch of the city's westernmost coastal road between Lincoln Way and Sloat Boulevard to vehicular traffic from Monday at 4 a.m. through Friday at 6 p.m., excluding holidays.</cite> <cite index="103-3,103-4,103-5">On Tuesday, the San Francisco City Controller's Office released an estimate of the costs of Proposition G. The measure would reopen the highway to vehicles on weekdays, reversing a 2024 measure approved by voters to close the highway for the creation of Sunset Dunes park. If approved, the controller's office found reopening the road would cost $9.8 million in one-time capital costs.</cite> <cite index="106-11,106-12">The annual costs of the ballot measure, if passed, would range from $500,000 to $1.9 million depending on the decisions made by city departments. Those costs include traffic signal maintenance, roadway maintenance and replacement, and sand removal and dune reshaping.</cite>

<cite index="22-8,22-9">Proponents of the measure, including Richard Correia, Albert Chow, District 4 Supervisor Alan Wong and grassroots volunteers, stood outside the Department of Elections in City Hall when signatures were filed. Wong said it's the most "contentious" issue in his neighborhood, and that the rest of the city did not realize its importance to the Westside when it was last at the ballot box in 2024.</cite>

<cite index="28-10">"This measure would destroy San Francisco's coastal park, requiring the City to tear out every park feature, and kill the 60% of park visits which happen on weekdays," said Lucas Lux, President of Friends of Sunset Dunes.</cite> <cite index="28-11">A majority of the Board of Supervisors oppose the measure, including Board President Rafael Mandelman, Matt Dorsey, Bilal Mahmood, Myrna Melgar, Danny Sauter and Stephen Sherrill.</cite> The election is November 3.

topStories.headline: Young Mountain Lion Roamed the Outer Sunset for Hours Before Wildlife Officers Captured and Released It
topStories.dek: A 78-pound male mountain lion spent the morning of September 18 under a house near 44th Avenue and Ulloa Street, triggering a multi-agency response, before being fitted with a GPS collar and returned to the Santa Cruz Mountains.
topStories.body:
<cite index="70-9,70-10,70-11">San Francisco police said officers were dispatched around 7:42 a.m. on September 18 to the 2500 block of 44th Avenue after receiving reports of a possible mountain lion. Officers located the animal near 44th Avenue and Ulloa Street and kept it in sight while waiting for other agencies to arrive. Police told nearby residents to shelter in place while officials handled the animal.</cite>

<cite index="71-3">The San Francisco Zoo helped tranquilize the animal after it took refuge beneath a bush in a residential neighborhood near 44th Avenue and Ulloa Street, according to San Francisco Animal Care and Control.</cite> <cite index="70-5">Fish and Wildlife spokesperson Peter Tira confirmed that the mountain lion was a young male, 2 to 3 years old, weighing about 78 pounds.</cite> <cite index="74-9,74-10">Eventually the cat became incapacitated and animal control officers removed it from the area just before noon. California Department of Fish and Wildlife veterinarians examined the mountain lion and gave it a clean bill of health before returning it to the wild Friday afternoon.</cite>

<cite index="70-4">The mountain lion captured Friday morning after wandering the streets of San Francisco's Outer Sunset neighborhood was released into wild habitat in the Santa Cruz Mountains, according to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife.</cite> <cite index="73-9">Officials said they are not sure where the mountain lion came from, but it could have traveled from the Peninsula, where there is habitat.</cite> <cite index="77-14,77-15">A mountain lion in San Francisco is still rare, and nobody was hurt. But it was the second sighting in two weeks, which makes it fair to ask what living on the city's wild edge involves.</cite>

moreNews.headline: Sunset Neighborway Network Stalls: Five Years In, Only One of Eight Promised Streets Is Done
moreNews.body: <cite index="120-8,120-9">The Sunset Neighborway project, aiming to add traffic-calming designs to eight residential streets, has only implemented street safety changes to one street after five years. Five years after being approved by the city, a "District 4 Family Neighborway Network" to make eight streets in the Sunset safer for pedestrians and cyclists has only finished one of them — Ortega Street.</cite> <cite index="120-11,120-12">Construction on Kirkham Street is still ongoing, while design and planning for 41st Avenue has been paused until late 2026. A lack of funding has put the other five streets on the shelf indefinitely.</cite> The Mission Local report published September 24 quoted an SFMTA spokesperson who cited the city's budget crisis as the primary cause of delays.

moreNews.headline: Hit-and-Run Pickup Destroys Four Parked Cars at Santiago Street and 28th Avenue in Parkside
moreNews.body: <cite index="90-5,90-6">A speeding pickup truck ran a stop sign and struck a parked car early Saturday in San Francisco's Parkside neighborhood, triggering a domino-like series of collisions that, ultimately, left four parked cars severely damaged. The dramatic predawn incident was caught on video.</cite> <cite index="90-7,90-8,90-9">Video shows the truck blowing through a four-way intersection at Santiago Street and 28th Avenue. After a loud bang, the driver backed up slightly and drove away. The first car struck — a silver Toyota — was hit at 2:36 a.m. on Saturday, its trunk hanging open and its back bumper dangling.</cite> The story was published by Mission Local on September 29; as of that Tuesday, two of the four damaged cars remained at the intersection and no arrest had been reported.

restaurants.name: San Tung

restaurants.name: Lavash
